tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (mph_test.go: BenchmarkTable vs BenchmarkTableMap, a Go map[string]uint32 over the same dictionary) and the README names the CPU (i7-8700K). The Go toolchain version and build flags are not stated, so this is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.caveats: The README does not state the Go toolchain version or build flags for the quoted ns/op numbers. It gives only the '-12' GOMAXPROCS suffix and the i7-8700K CPU. The numbers were added to the README on 2021-09-01, so they were measured against the Go map that existed before Go 1.24, which replaced the built-in map with a Swiss-table design. The 27% gap may therefore not hold on current Go. The benchmark reads the host's /usr/share/dict/words, so the key set depends on the machine. The numbers are first-party and have not been reproduced independently.

notes: The claim is accurate: the README shows 29.99 ns/op vs 40.92 ns/op, and the derived 27% matches. Only last_commit needed a fix: the record used the repo's pushed_at (2023-01-22), but the newest commit on the only branch (main, 14a3196) is dated 2021-09-01. It is still 'abandoned'. The README numbers and go.mod (`go 1.17`) were added in the same 2021-09-01 commits, but the README never names the toolchain, so compiler_and_flags was left as is.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (src/benchmark.zig, run through the build.zig `benchmark` step with zBench). The README states the compiler (Zig 0.15.1), the flags (`zig build benchmark --release=fast`, i.e. ReleaseFast) and the CPU (Intel Core i7-8750H), so all A criteria are met.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.1; zig build benchmark --release=fast (ReleaseFast optimize mode)
corrections.workload: A PerfectHashMap built at runtime (PerfectHashMap.init with an allocator, not the comptimeInit path) over the words in the host's /usr/share/dict/words (word count not stated), compared with Zig std.StringHashMap and std.StaticStringMap, both also built at runtime. zBench runs 100,000 lookups per structure and times each run individually. The build (construction) time of each structure is also measured.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Lookup (zBench average of single-call runs): zmph 26ns ± 4ns vs std.StringHashMap 45ns ± 152ns (README: StringHashMap is ~1.7x slower than zmph) and vs std.StaticStringMap 10.4us ± 7.359us (README: ~400x slower, which the README attributes to binary search). Build: zmph 28.872ms vs StringHashMap 6.1ms (~5x slower to build) and StaticStringMap 2.029ms (~14x slower to build).
corrections.caveats: The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub license is null), so it is reference-only. The benchmark is first-party and was run on one machine. Each zBench run wraps a single lookup (an indirect call) in std.time.Timer start/read, so fixed timer overhead is part of both the 26 ns and the 45 ns figures, and the true lookup-cost ratio is uncertain. StringHashMap's σ is 152 ns (max 29.795 us). The ~400x StaticStringMap gap is not a fair comparison: in Zig 0.15.1, StaticStringMap.getIndex scans all keys of the same length linearly (it does not do a binary search, as the README says), and it is designed for small keyword sets, not a large dictionary. The benchmark measures runtime init, not the compile-time comptimeInit path that the README headlines. The results have not been reproduced independently.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly, and tier A holds. For the catalog, the headline should be the ~1.7x win over std.StringHashMap. The 400x win over StaticStringMap comes from using a linear-scan structure on a dictionary-sized key set (checked in the Zig 0.15.1 static_string_map.zig source). The record left out the Zig version and wrongly called the benchmarked map 'comptime-built'; both are fixed. Metadata is correct: no license, 8 stars, last commit 2026-01-31, active, not a fork.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (crates/lute/benches/common/mod.rs, lute.rs and phf.rs at commit d7f32c21a0, using divan), and BENCHMARKS.md names both CPUs. The rustc version and flags are not stated, so this is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Query (derived from page data: values read from the SVG plot marker coordinates against the labeled log-scale axes; lute 0.1.0 vs phf 0.14.0; u64, short-string and long shared-prefix-string keys; n=1..65535; hits and misses): Median isolated per-query latency is 1.9x-9.8x lower than phf. On the Ryzen 9 9950X the range is 2.6x-9.8x, e.g. u64 n=2048 hit ~1.73 ns vs ~8.04 ns and long strings n=65535 hit ~11.4 ns vs ~30.6 ns. On the Apple M1 Pro the range is 1.9x-9.7x. Median amortized time per query is 1.9x-16.9x lower (9950X 2.6x-10.4x; M1 Pro 1.9x-16.9x, largest for u64 at n<=10). Lute is faster than phf at every plotted point in both query charts. Construction (the PHF-search time only) is mixed. Lute is 2.7x-8.3x faster at n=1-4 (up to ~10.5x for u64 n=8) and about even to ~2.3x faster for u64 sets with n>=4096. It is slower at many other sizes, e.g. about 0.5x-0.8x of phf's speed for short strings at n=128-16384 on the 9950X. The worst spike is ~120x slower (long strings, n=9, 9950X: ~44.9 us vs ~0.37 us).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with the divan harness and the default bench profile. The rustc version and RUSTFLAGS are not stated; the workspace MSRV is rust-version 1.88.
corrections.workload: Immutable maps/sets for fixed collections of up to 65535 entries, which can be built at compile time with macros or build-script codegen. BENCHMARKS.md has plots for three key types: u64, short strings and long shared-prefix strings. The plotted sizes are n=1..65535 (25 sizes). The plots cover PHF-search construction time, median isolated per-query latency (#[inline(never)]) and median amortized time per query (a shuffled all-hit or all-miss stream), all vs the phf crate. In the benchmark, the phf maps are built at runtime to mirror what phf_codegen emits.
corrections.caveats: The numbers exist only as SVG plots, with the text converted to glyph paths. The values in claimed_speedup were read from the plot marker coordinates, so they are approximate. The rustc version and flags are not stated. The plots are dated 2026-06-22 (lute 0.1.0/0.1.1, phf 0.14.0) and match the benchmark code at commit d7f32c21a0. Since then, the unreleased HEAD has replaced CHD displacement with a PTHash/PtrHash-style pilot table and a 'packed' strategy and changed the benchmark sizes, so the plots do not reflect HEAD. HEAD also adds a hashbrown comparison, which has no published plots. Construction time is not a win over phf. GitHub reports only Apache-2.0, but Cargo.toml and the README declare MIT OR Apache-2.0, and both LICENSE files are present. The project is first-party with 4 stars, and the results have not been reproduced independently.

notes: The record said the plot numbers could not be extracted. I recovered them by rendering the six SVGs and reading the marker coordinates on the labeled log axes, calibrated to the 1 ns/10 ns and 10 ns/100 ns gridlines. Lute wins on every query point by 1.9x-16.9x, while construction is mixed. Tier C holds because the toolchain and flags are missing. Metadata is correct: license MIT OR Apache-2.0, 4 stars, last commit 2026-08-18, active, not a fork.
